extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism researchers, and journalists interested in news selection/newsworthiness
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and organizes the factors Östgaard (1965) identifies as influencing the flow of news — the criteria that make events more or less likely to be selected and transmitted by news organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplification
rubrics_metrics.description: To be transmitted quickly through the news chain, an event must be simplifiable; the greater the complexity, the lower the news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implications given: stories with clear causation are favored over those requiring background; discrete events are preferred to ongoing processes; single actors are easier to report than diffuse collectives. In practice, reporters and editors prefer events that can be told succinctly and fit standard story structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences must be able to identify with the event for it to be news; identification increases an event's news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subcomponents and guidance: cultural proximity (events from similar cultures are preferred), eliteness (stories about elite persons/nations help readers locate themselves), personification (personalizing events makes identification easier), and status-quo orientation (events that fit existing audience worldviews are preferred over those that challenge them). Use identification to assess audience resonance and perceived relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: News competes for attention; dramatic, shocking, or conflict-laden material is more newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes specific elements: conflict (disputes, fights, wars), drama (high-stakes outcomes), and negativity (bad news attracts attention). Stories exhibiting these features are more likely to be selected and amplified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical/Cultural Distance (News Barrier)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events become less newsworthy as physical and cultural distance from the audience increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geographical and cultural remoteness reduces selection likelihood. Proximity increases perceived relevance and ease of coverage; distance imposes both perceptual and logistical barriers to transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic Barriers (News Barrier)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events from outside the audience's language area face friction and are less likely to be covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language differences raise costs and friction in reporting (translation, sourcing), which decreases an event's newsworthiness in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource Concentration (News Barrier)
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations and reporting resources concentrate in capitals and elite cities, creating barriers for events occurring elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because reporters, wire services, and infrastructure cluster in certain places, events in peripheral locations are underreported. This concentration contributes to systematic bias toward elites and major centers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political Factors (Foreign-to-the-Process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Government interests, censorship, and foreign-policy alignments influence what events are promoted or suppressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State-level priorities and restrictions can actively shape news flow by encouraging coverage of favored issues, limiting access to others, or imposing censorship. Consider how official narratives and diplomatic concerns alter selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic Factors (Foreign-to-the-Process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs of newsgathering, advertising and audience pressures, and ownership interests shape coverage; cheaper-to-cover stories are preferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic incentives — e.g., resource limits, advertising dependence, ownership editorial influence — push organizations toward stories that maximize audience/advertising value and minimize expense. Cost and marketability are practical selection criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implications for Newsworthiness (Cumulative Bias & Elite Concentration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Östgaard argues that the listed factors cumulatively distort the 'news picture' of the world, producing systematic bias and concentrating coverage on simple, dramatic, near, and elite-centered events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as an evaluative lens: consider not just single factors but their cumulative effect when assessing how accurately coverage represents reality. Predicts elite concentration and systematic underrepresentation of complex, remote, or non-personified processes.
